subject: Flat August GDP, two days after the BoC hiked
bodyMarkdown:
The Bank of Canada raised interest rates on Wednesday. On Friday, Statistics Canada reported that the economy had not grown at all in August, the second flat month in a row. If you carry a variable mortgage, work in wholesale or manufacturing, or hold Canadian bank shares, the next six weeks come down to which of those two facts the Bank decides to believe.

## What Friday's numbers said

Statistics Canada reported Friday that real GDP was essentially unchanged in August. Economists had looked for a gain of 0.2 per cent, and so had the agency's own earlier **flash estimate**, the quick guess it publishes for a month it has not finished counting. Wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent, with most subsectors contracting. Federal public administration shrank as work on the 2026 Census wound down, which is a one-time drag rather than a sign of anything. Mining and quarrying rose 4.9 per cent, and retail trade bounced back. The line I keep rereading is the September one: Statistics Canada's early estimate points to a decline of 0.1 per cent, with manufacturing and the oil and gas sector leading the way down. Two flat months and a negative one is not a recession. It is also not an economy with much give in it.

## The Bank hiked first, then saw this

Governing Council raised the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent on Wednesday, the first increase since 2023, putting the Bank Rate at 2.75 per cent and the deposit rate at 2.45 per cent. The reasoning was about inflation rather than growth. The Bank said its inflation outlook had deteriorated and that it expects global oil prices to stay higher for longer, and its October projection has inflation sitting near 3 per cent through much of 2027. Governor Tiff Macklem said further increases might be needed and that the Bank would move carefully. Andrew Grantham at CIBC, quoted by BNN Bloomberg on Friday, said the August figures showed an economy that "was already struggling for momentum even before this week's interest rate hike." My read is that the Bank sees oil-driven price pressure as the risk it can still do something about, and a soft economy as the price.

## The loonie went up anyway

Here is the part that surprised me. The Canadian dollar rose on Friday instead of falling. The Globe and Mail reported Friday that the loonie traded near a six-week high, because higher oil prices lifted bets on further Bank of Canada increases, which overshadowed the weak GDP release, and that the currency was heading for its biggest monthly gain since April. Canadian bond yields went the other way, easing across a steeper curve as a selloff in technology shares sent money into U.S. Treasuries. So the currency market is betting the Bank keeps tightening while the bond market quietly hedges a slowdown. Both cannot be right on December 9, when the next decision lands. My guess is the Bank holds at 2.5 per cent and talks tough, which is the cheapest move available to a central bank whose own forecast is in question.

## The takeaway

Watch the October jobs report and the September GDP figure, because both arrive before the December 9 decision and either one could settle the argument. If you are renewing a mortgage in the next few months, price it as though 2.5 per cent is a floor you sit on for a while rather than a stop on the way back down, because the Bank's own inflation path leaves no room for cuts next year. A flat economy next to a 3 per cent inflation forecast is an awkward pair, closer to **stagflation** (weak growth and sticky prices at the same time) than to anything comfortable. I will be reading the September number closely.
